hook_text: Three bikes: R1 850, R1 580, R1 805. Which is cheapest? You can tell in two digits.
clip_script: Market in Polokwane. Three bikes: R1 850, R1 580, R1 805. Which is cheapest? Do not add anything. Count the digits: four each. Look left: all have 1 thousand. Next digit: 8, 5, 8. The 5 loses, so R1 580 is cheapest. The other two tie on hundreds, so look at tens: 5 against 0. R1 850 is the most expensive. That is comparing: biggest question first, from the left. Now odd or even. 1 085: is it odd? Look at the last digit only. 5. Odd. 1 000? Ends in 0. Even. Never add the digits, never look at the first digit. The last digit decides. Two tricks: compare from the left, test odd or even from the right.
visual_style: Whiteboard price tags with digits lighting up one column at a time from the left; a street with even houses on one side and odd on the other.
pacing: Three bikes compared in ten seconds, then the odd-even test, then the two-trick rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sort the prices in a shop catalogue from cheapest to dearest.
